title: Caching
subtitle: Reduce repeated work with fast copies while controlling staleness and invalidation
objectives: Explain why caching works at all — and why it's a bet on skewed traffic, not on cache size
Wire a cache correctly: cache-aside, the write patterns, and local vs shared
Reason about eviction, and read the miss rate rather than the hit rate
Diagnose the hard parts: invalidation, stampedes, the stale-set race, and a cache that's quietly load-bearing

exercises.title: A cache stores reusable results on a faster read path
exercises.body: A cache maps a lookup key to a previously computed value. A request checks that key first. A hit returns the stored value; a miss runs the database query or API call, returns its result, and may store a copy for later requests.
exercises.note: Caching reduces backend work only when requests reuse keys. A workload with mostly unique keys produces misses while still paying the cache lookup and storage cost.

exercises.prompt: A database receives 10,000 identical product reads per second but handles 2,000. Put a cache in the read path with a 90% hit rate.
exercises.result: Cache hits removed 9,000 repeated database reads
exercises.why: At a 90% hit rate, only 10% of 10,000 reads reach the database, reducing its load to 1,000 reads/s. Correctness still requires an expiry or invalidation policy when product data changes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A database receives 10,000 identical product reads per second but handles 2,000. Put a cache in the read path with a 90% hit rate. Place Cache, Database. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Clients → Cache; Cache → Database. That topology is the evidence for the answer: At a 90% hit rate, only 10% of 10,000 reads reach the database, reducing its load to 1,000 reads/s. Correctness still requires an expiry or invalidation policy when product data changes.

exercises.prompt: Your product page runs the same expensive database query 10,000 times a second. Every single run returns an identical result. What's the cheapest fix?
choices: Buy a faster database
Run the query once, keep the answer somewhere fast, and hand out that copy
Add more application servers
Ask users to refresh less often
exercises.why: Caching stores the query result after one execution and serves that copy to later requests, removing 9,999 repeated database executions while the result remains reusable. The benefit depends on repeated requests for the same answer; unique results would continue to miss.

exercises.prompt: A ______ stores the result of expensive work so the next request gets the answer without redoing it.
choices: cache
queue
replica
index
exercises.why: A cache records the output of previous work under a key. A later lookup for that key can return the stored output without repeating the database query or computation, and eviction may remove the entry when space or freshness policy requires it.

exercises.prompt: Your database holds 50 million products. Your cache holds 50,000 — one thousandth of them. Why isn't that hopeless?
choices: Because the cache is faster, so it makes up the difference
Because requests aren't spread evenly — a small set of products gets asked for constantly, and that set fits
Because the cache compresses the data
Because 50,000 is enough for most databases
exercises.why: Request popularity is commonly skewed: a small hot set receives a large share of reads. If the 50,000 most-requested products fit, the cache can answer most traffic despite storing only 0.1% of the catalog; a uniform request distribution would produce little reuse.

exercises.prompt: Match each read to roughly what it costs (order-of-magnitude, not precise).

pairs.left: Cache over the network, same datacenter

exercises.why: Local memory avoids a network round trip and is measured in nanoseconds. A shared cache adds datacenter networking and protocol processing, an indexed solid-state-drive query adds storage and database work, and an intercontinental round trip is dominated by propagation distance. These orders of magnitude determine which saved operation makes caching valuable.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good things to cache? Select all.
choices: A product page that changes twice a year and is viewed a million times a day
The same shared dashboard report, requested with identical inputs by every user and allowed to be 5 minutes stale
A user's current account balance, read to decide whether a transfer clears
A 'trending now' feed that's expensive to compute and fine a minute out of date
exercises.why: The product page, shared report, and trending feed reuse expensive results and tolerate their stated update frequency. A balance used to authorize a transfer requires the current source-of-truth value because a stale copy can approve spending unavailable funds; that read is unsuitable for this cache path.

exercises.prompt: You add a cache. What have you unavoidably introduced?
choices: A second copy of the data that is allowed to disagree with the source of truth
A slower system
A new database
Nothing — it's a pure win
exercises.why: The database remains the source of truth while the cache stores a derived copy. Writes can change the database before the cached value is updated or removed, so the two can disagree for a period defined by invalidation and expiry policy.

exercises.title: Cache-aside makes the application responsible for loading cached values
exercises.body: For a cache-aside read, the application looks up a key in the cache. On a miss, it reads the database, stores the returned value under that key, and responds. Application code coordinates the cache and database as two independent dependencies.
exercises.note: During normal operation, the database receives the cache-miss fraction. During a cache outage, direct reads make it absorb total request traffic.

exercises.prompt: Five API servers miss the same expired product key simultaneously, causing five identical database reads. Collapse concurrent misses per server.
choices: Increase the cache TTL forever
Use one in-flight load per key
Add a database read replica
choiceFeedback: An infinite TTL avoids expiry by accepting unbounded staleness; invalidation and cold keys still exist.
Single-flight coalescing makes concurrent callers in this process share one database load.
A replica adds read capacity, but all five identical reads still execute.
exercises.beforeStatus: ONE EXPIRED KEY · 5 database reads from this server process
exercises.afterStatus: ONE EXPIRED KEY · 1 database read · 5 callers share result
exercises.result: Concurrent callers joined one in-flight load
exercises.why: Request coalescing lets concurrent callers in one process await the same in-flight cache fill. In a multi-server fleet, each server may still issue one load unless coordination occurs at a shared layer.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Five API servers miss the same expired product key simultaneously, causing five identical database reads. Collapse concurrent misses per server. Place Single-flight map, Database. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: 5 callers → Single-flight map; Single-flight map → Database. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Request coalescing lets concurrent callers in one process await the same in-flight cache fill. In a multi-server fleet, each server may still issue one load unless coordination occurs at a shared layer.

exercises.prompt: Order a cache-aside read — the most common wiring.
steps: App asks the cache for key 'product:42'
Cache misses — it doesn't have it
App writes the result into the cache
App returns the result to the user
exercises.why: In cache-aside, the application first looks up the key, queries the database after a miss, stores the returned value, and then responds. The cache does not fetch from the database itself, and an unavailable cache can be bypassed if the application and database have capacity for direct reads.

exercises.prompt: Cache-aside is also called ______ loading, because an item only enters the cache when someone actually asks for it.
choices: lazy
eager
write
bulk
exercises.why: Lazy loading inserts an item only after a request misses and retrieves it from the source. This lets real demand select cached entries, while the first request for each absent item pays the source cost and a cold cache can send a large miss burst downstream.

exercises.prompt: Match each caching pattern to how it works.

pairs.right: App checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the DB itself
App only talks to the cache; the cache loads from the DB on a miss
Writes go to cache and DB together, before the write is acknowledged
Writes land in the cache and flush to the DB later

exercises.why: Cache-aside makes the application load misses, while read-through gives that responsibility to the cache layer. Write-through acknowledges after updating both cache and database, adding write latency; write-behind acknowledges from the cache and persists later, creating a durability window.

exercises.prompt: Build the write-behind path. Place the component that acknowledges first and the durable authority that receives the write later.
exercises.why: The write-behind cache acknowledges before asynchronously flushing the change to the database, which remains the durable authority. If the cache loses the pending entry or the flush fails after acknowledgement, the database never receives the write and the user loses data they were told was saved.

exercises.prompt: Build the read path: the app should check for a saved answer *before* doing the expensive work.
exercises.why: The application must query the cache before the database so a hit can bypass the expensive database read. On a miss, the request continues to the database and the result can populate the cache for later reuse.

exercises.prompt: You use cache-aside at a 95% hit rate. Your Redis cluster dies completely, at peak traffic. What happens?
choices: Every request goes straight to the database — which suddenly takes 20× its normal read load and may fall over
The app crashes
Writes fail
Nothing changes
exercises.why: At a 95% hit rate, the database normally receives the 5% miss stream. Complete cache loss turns every read into a miss, increasing database read load from 5% to 100% of traffic, a 20-fold jump that can exceed its capacity even though cache-aside remains logically correct.

exercises.prompt: You cache in each app server's own memory instead of a shared Redis. What's the catch?
choices: It's slower than a shared cache
Each server has its own copy — so they can disagree with each other, and every server must warm up separately
It can't store structured objects
There's no catch
exercises.why: An in-process cache gives each app server an independent copy. Invalidations and warm-up therefore occur separately, so requests routed to different servers can observe different values and every restart begins cold; a shared cache adds a network hop but centralizes the cached entry.

lessons.title: Eviction & the hit rate that matters

exercises.title: The miss rate determines how much read traffic reaches the backend
exercises.body: For read rate R and hit rate H, the cache answers R × H requests and the backend receives R × (1 − H) misses. At 10,000 reads/s and 95% hits, the cache serves 9,500 reads/s while the database still executes 500 reads/s.
exercises.note: Backend capacity must cover the miss stream. Small hit-rate gains near 100% can sharply reduce backend load because that load scales with the remaining miss rate.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: The miss rate determines how much read traffic reaches the backend
exercises.why: For read rate R and hit rate H, the cache answers R × H requests and the backend receives R × (1 − H) misses. At 10,000 reads/s and 95% hits, the cache serves 9,500 reads/s while the database still executes 500 reads/s. Backend capacity must cover the miss stream. Small hit-rate gains near 100% can sharply reduce backend load because that load scales with the remaining miss rate.

exercises.prompt: Read traffic is 20,000 req/s. Your database tops out at 2,000 req/s before it falls over. Drag the hit rate to the *lowest* setting that keeps it alive.
exercises.why: At a 90% hit rate, the 10% miss stream sends 2,000 of the 20,000 requests per second to the database, exactly its capacity. Raising the hit rate to 99% lowers the miss stream to 200 requests per second, so a nine-point hit-rate increase cuts database load by a factor of ten.

exercises.prompt: Your cache's memory fills up. A new item needs to go in. What has to happen?
choices: Something already in the cache gets thrown out to make room
The cache grows itself to fit
The item is stored on disk instead
The oldest item moves back to the database
exercises.why: Finite cache memory cannot retain every new entry. Eviction selects an existing entry to remove so the new one can be stored; the policy affects hit rate by deciding which values remain available for reuse.

exercises.prompt: Match each eviction policy to what it throws out.

pairs.right: Whatever hasn't been touched for the longest
Whatever gets asked for least often
Anything past its expiry, popular or not

exercises.why: Least recently used (`LRU`) removes the entry with the oldest access, least frequently used (LFU) removes the lowest access count, time to live (`TTL`) expires entries after a freshness interval, and random chooses without access history. `LRU` and LFU manage capacity using reuse signals; `TTL` primarily bounds staleness.

exercises.prompt: Your `LRU` cache holds the 50,000 hottest products at a 96% hit rate. A nightly job starts reading all 50 million products once, in order. What happens?
choices: Nothing — the job's reads get cached too
The hit rate collapses: every scanned item counts as 'recently used', so the scan evicts the entire hot set for data nobody will ask for again
It improves — more data is now cached
The cache rejects the job's reads
exercises.why: A sequential scan marks each one-time item as recently used, so `LRU` evicts frequently reused products to admit scan entries. This cache pollution replaces the hot set with values unlikely to be requested again, collapsing the hit rate until normal traffic rebuilds the set.

exercises.prompt: A cache has a 95% hit rate. Hits contribute 0.95ms to the average read latency, while the 5% of requests that miss contribute 5ms, for a 5.95ms total. What should you optimize first?
choices: The 1ms hit path, because it handles most requests
The miss rate or 100ms miss path, because misses contribute about 84% of the average latency
Both paths contribute equally
Neither path affects average latency
exercises.why: Misses contribute 5ms of the 5.95ms average, about 84%, even though they are only 5% of requests. Reducing the miss rate or the 100ms miss cost therefore has much more leverage on average latency than making the 1ms hit path slightly faster.

exercises.prompt: Your hit rate is 90%. You tune it to 99%. That's only 9 points. Why is it actually enormous?
choices: It isn't — 9% is marginal
Because the misses are what cost you: 10% → 1% is one tenth as many misses, so one tenth the database load
Because the cache got faster
Because 99% is a round number
exercises.why: A 90% hit rate leaves a 10% miss rate, while a 99% hit rate leaves a 1% miss rate. Database reads follow misses, so the change sends one tenth as many requests to the database even though the hit rate rose by only nine percentage points.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually raise your hit RATE? Select all.
choices: More cache memory, so the hot set fits
A longer `TTL`, so entries live long enough to be reused
Keeping batch scans off the cache so they can't evict the hot set
A faster network to the cache
exercises.why: More memory keeps a larger hot set, a longer `TTL` gives entries more time to be reused, and excluding scans prevents one-time reads from evicting hot entries. Faster networking reduces hit latency but does not change whether a lookup finds its key; longer expiry also increases the permitted staleness window.

exercises.prompt: You set a 60-second `TTL` on a cached value. What have you actually decided?
choices: That the value takes 60 seconds to compute
That you're willing to serve data up to 60 seconds out of date
That the value will be refreshed every 60 seconds
That the cache holds 60 seconds of data
exercises.why: A 60-second time to live (`TTL`) keeps a cached copy eligible for 60 seconds after storage, so a source update can remain hidden until that interval ends. Expiry marks the entry ineligible. With lazy loading, the first read after expiry fetches the source value and repopulates the cache.

exercises.title: Correct cache invalidation needs dependency mapping and race control
exercises.body: A source row may feed several cached keys, so writes must identify every dependent key. A concurrent miss can also read old data and repopulate the cache after invalidation. Leases, version checks, or equivalent ordering prevent stale resurrection; a time-to-live bounds residual failures.
exercises.note: An omitted dependency or lost ordering signal can serve stale data silently. A time-to-live limits the stale window but does not establish correctness.

exercises.prompt: Phil Karlton's famous line: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Why is invalidation genuinely hard?
choices: Deleting a key is computationally expensive
Knowing WHICH keys a change affects — and finding all of them — is the hard part, and getting it wrong is silent
Caches don't support deletion
It requires taking the cache offline
exercises.why: One source value may contribute to several cache keys, such as a product page, category listing, search result, and homepage module. An update must identify and invalidate every affected derived value. Any missed dependency continues serving a syntactically valid stale response, which makes the defect difficult to detect.

exercises.prompt: On a write, should you update the cached value or just delete it?
choices: Update it — that keeps the cache warm
Usually delete it: updating computes a value nobody asked for, and races with other writers over whose version lands last
Neither — let the `TTL` handle it
Both, for safety
exercises.why: Deleting marks the cached answer absent, so the next read rebuilds it from the source of truth. Updating can compute an unused value and allows concurrent writers to place cache updates in a different order from database commits, leaving a stale value resident.

exercises.prompt: A homepage key receives 10,000 requests/sec, takes 200ms to rebuild, and just expired. Without request coalescing or a lock, how many rebuilds can overlap?
choices: About 200
About 2,000
Exactly 10,000
Only one
exercises.why: Concurrency is arrival rate multiplied by rebuild time: 10,000 requests/second × 0.2 seconds = about 2,000 overlapping rebuilds. Requests arriving during that window independently see the miss, creating a cache stampede; coalescing or a per-key lock lets one rebuild run while others wait.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually help against a cache stampede? Select all.
choices: A lock, so only the first request rebuilds and the others wait for it
Serve the stale value while one request refreshes it in the background
Add jitter to TTLs so a batch of keys doesn't all expire in the same instant
Shorten the `TTL` so it happens more often but costs less each time
exercises.why: A per-key lock lets one request rebuild while peers wait, and serving stale data lets peers respond while one refresh runs. Jitter randomizes expiries so many keys do not create synchronized miss bursts. Shorter `TTL` values increase expiry frequency without limiting how many requests race after one expiry.

exercises.prompt: Two things happen at once. Request A misses and reads value V1 from the database. Before A writes it back, request B writes V2 to the database and deletes the cache key — which is already empty, so that's a no-op. Then A writes V1 into the cache. What's the state?
choices: The cache holds V2 — correct
The cache holds V1 while the database holds V2, and the invalidation already happened, so nothing will fix it until the `TTL` expires
The cache is empty
A's write fails
exercises.why: Request A read V1 before request B committed V2. B's deletion occurred while the key was absent, then A populated the cache with its older result, leaving V1 cached over database value V2. A version check or lease can reject A's stale population; otherwise expiry provides the eventual backstop.

exercises.prompt: A cached product price must be no more than 60 seconds stale even if write-triggered invalidation fails. What is the longest safe `TTL`?
exercises.why: A 60-second time to live bounds staleness to 60 seconds after a missed invalidation; any longer value violates the freshness service-level objective. With 200 active cache nodes, this TTL would average about 200 ÷ 60 = 3.3 refreshes per second when each node refreshes independently.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of caching?
choices: It makes your system fast for free
It buys latency and backend relief by keeping a second copy that's allowed to be wrong — and hands you invalidation, eviction, stampedes, and a component your system now secretly depends on
It's only needed above millions of users
It removes the need for a fast database
exercises.why: Caching reduces latency and backend read load when expensive results are reused and can tolerate bounded staleness. The cached copy introduces eviction, invalidation races, stampedes, and failure amplification: at a 95% hit rate, losing the cache raises database read traffic from 5% to 100%, a 20-fold increase.

exercises.prompt: An authorization cache says Alice may read a report. Access is revoked in the database, but the cached decision lives for ten minutes. What is the failure?
choices: Stale cached authorization permits access after revocation
The database becomes unavailable
The cache increases write durability
TLS expires
exercises.why: The cached copy outlives the authoritative policy change. Security-sensitive caches need bounded staleness and an invalidation or version strategy matching the revocation requirement.
